input.capability: Explain and add fractions by reasoning about equal-sized parts.
input.environment: Prepared presentation fixture; no model or external research is invoked.

exit_criteria.text: Use a common unit to explain a new fraction sum.

variants.question: A friend says 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9. Explain the error and find the sum.
variants.answer: Use sixths: 1/3 = 2/6, so 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Adding denominators does not keep a common-sized unit.
required: rename one third as two sixths
sum is three sixths or one half

input.objective: Explain why the parts counted by a fraction must be equal-sized.
input.why_needed: Without a common-sized unit, counting pieces does not describe an amount.
input.motivation: Cut a pizza into four unequal pieces. Is every piece one quarter?
outline: The denominator describes that partition; the numerator counts parts.

misconceptions.text: Any one of four pieces is one quarter.
misconceptions.repair: Compare a tiny slice with a slice covering half the same pizza.

variants.question: A cake is cut into four unequal pieces. Is each piece one quarter? Explain.
variants.answer: No. Quarters are four equal-sized parts of the same whole.

variants.question: What must be true of eight pieces for each to be one eighth?
variants.answer: They must be eight equal-sized parts of the same whole.

hints: What does the denominator tell you about the size of one part?
Imagine the same whole divided into equal-sized pieces.
Rename the amount in equal-sized pieces before comparing or combining it.

input.objective: Explain why one half and two quarters describe the same amount.
input.why_needed: A common denominator renames an amount; it does not make the amount larger.
input.motivation: Split each of two equal halves in half again. What changed?
outline: Start with one of two equal parts.
Split every part into two equal subparts.
Twice as many selected pieces, each half as large, preserves the amount.

misconceptions.text: Two quarters is larger because two is larger than one.
misconceptions.repair: Use one unchanged whole; show the selected area before and after splitting.

variants.question: Why is 1/2 equal to 2/4, rather than smaller?
variants.answer: Each half is split into two quarters. Twice as many half-sized pieces preserve the amount of the same whole.
required: twice as many pieces preserve the same amount

variants.question: Explain why 2/3 and 4/6 name the same amount.
variants.answer: Each third is split into two sixths; twice as many half-sized pieces preserve the same amount.
required: twice as many pieces preserve the same amount

input.objective: Add one half and one quarter by expressing both in quarters.
input.why_needed: Counting unlike units together gives the wrong total.
input.motivation: You ate half of a cake and then another quarter of the same cake.
outline: Rename one half as two quarters.
Add two quarters and one quarter.
The result is three quarters, not two sixths.

misconceptions.text: Add the numerators and denominators separately.
misconceptions.repair: Ask what size of piece a sixth would be and why the original pieces did not become sixths.

variants.question: What is 1/2 + 1/4? Explain why the denominator stays four.
variants.answer: 1/2 is 2/4, so 2/4 + 1/4 is 3/4. We are counting quarter-sized pieces.
required: rename one half as two quarters
three quarter-sized pieces give three quarters
